Toward Safe LLM Agents: A Survey of Specification, Verification, and Enforcement Pierre Dantas Affiliation: The University of Manchester Affiliation: Manchester, UK Email: pierre.dantas@manchester.ac.uk Lucas Cordeiro Affiliation: The University of Manchester Affiliation: Manchester, UK Email: lucas.cordeiro@manchester.ac.uk Ehsan Nowroozi Affiliation: The University of Greenwich Affiliation: London, UK Email: ehsan.nowroozi65@ieee.org Tihanyi Norbert Affiliation: Technology Innovation Institute Affiliation: Abu Dhabi, UAE Email: ntihanyi@inf.elte.hu Abstract Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly perform irreversible real-world actions, including database updates, API calls, file operations, and autonomous use of tools. However, no existing system provides formally grounded, task-level safety guarantees for the plans these agents generate. Research remains fragmented across specification, verification, and enforcement, limiting understanding of the strengths and limitations of existing approaches. To address this gap, we conducted a PRISMA 2020 systematic review of 38 studies published between 2022 and 2026 and retrieved from six academic databases. Our analysis reveals four key findings. First, the specification bottleneck remains the primary challenge: natural-language-to-formal translation achieves only 24 % to 35 % 24	ext{\,}\mathrm{\%}35	ext{\,}\mathrm{\%} semantic correctness, undermining downstream verification. Second, runtime monitoring is the most mature enforcement strategy, reducing unsafe actions by 40 % to 65 % 40	ext{\,}\mathrm{\%}65	ext{\,}\mathrm{\%} in controlled settings, but it does not provide complete safety guarantees. Third, the verifier tax shows that blocking 94 % 94	ext{\,}\mathrm{\%} of unsafe actions can still result in less than 5 % 5	ext{\,}\mathrm{\%} safe task completion because agents exploit alternative unsafe paths. Finally, no existing approach simultaneously achieves soundness, scalability, semantic correctness, and task-level safety preservation. We contribute a three-level taxonomy, a comparative analysis of existing techniques, a synthesis of evidence on the verifier tax, and a ten-problem research agenda for trustworthy agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) . K eywords Agentic AI, formal verification, runtime monitoring, safety guarantees, model checking, specification languages 1 Introduction Large Language Model (LLM) agents – systems in which an LLM serves as a reasoning engine that selects and sequences tool calls, sub-tasks, or robotic actions – have moved rapidly from research prototypes to production deployments. They now operate in consequential settings including software engineering [ 1 ] , healthcare [ 2 ] , customer service [ 3 ] , and autonomous driving [ 4 ] . In each of these domains, an agent’s plan – the sequence of actions it commits to executing – can have irreversible real-world effects: a misconfigured deployment, an erroneous medication recommendation, an unauthorized financial transaction, a collision. The fundamental safety challenge is that LLMs generate plans through statistical pattern matching over training data, rather than through sound logical inference. A plan that reads fluently and appears coherent may violate safety invariants, disregard temporal ordering constraints (e.g., authentication must precede data access), or produce cascading harmful effects that are individually plausible yet collectively catastrophic. This survey empirically documents this gap: none of 16 popular LLM agents scored above 60 % 60	ext{\,}\mathrm{\%} on a structured safety benchmark spanning 2,000 test cases [ 5 ] . Frontier models show limited robustness even to basic jailbreak attacks in multi-step agentic settings [ 6 ] . Classical Artificial Intelligence (AI) planning as well as formal verification offer mathematically rigorous tools for guaranteeing plan correctness: Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) -based planners, model checkers such as Simple Promela Interpreter (SPIN) and New Symbolic Model Verifier (NuSMV) , and deductive verifiers such as Dafny and Coq. However, applying these tools to LLM agent outputs requires closing the gap between unstructured Natural Language (NL) and formal mathematical structures – a non-trivial translation problem that, in itself, introduces semantic errors. The consequence is a specification-verification-enforcement pipeline for LLM agent plans that is fragile at every stage: specifications may be semantically incorrect [ 7 ] , verification may operate over inaccurate formal models [ 8 ] , and enforcement may block unsafe single actions while leaving task-level safety unresolved [ 9 ] . This survey systematically maps the emerging literature that attempts to close this gap. We cover the period 2022 to 2026, encompassing the LLM -agent era from GPT-3/4 onward, and identify 38 studies across the specification, verification, enforcement, and evaluation subfields using a PRISMA 2020 systematic review protocol. 1.1 Problem Statement We define the formal validation problem for LLM agent plans as follows. Let 𝒜 \mathcal{A} be an LLM -based agent that, given a task description t t and an observation history h h , generates a plan π = ( a 1 , a 2 , … , a n ) \pi=(a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{n}) where each a i a_{i} is an action (tool call, sub-task delegation, or physical action). Let φ \varphi be a safety property expressed in a formal system ℒ \mathcal{L} . The verification task is to determine whether π ⊧ φ \pi\models\varphi – whether the plan satisfies the property – before, during, or after execution, and to enforce compliance when it does not, as illustrated in Figure 1 . This partition reveals three tightly coupled sub-problems: 1. Specification: How is φ \varphi acquired from human-expressible requirements and represented in ℒ \mathcal{L} ? 2. Verification: How is π ⊧ φ \pi\models\varphi determined efficiently and soundly, given that π \pi is generated stochastically and may be open-ended? 3. Enforcement: What action is taken when π ⊧̸ φ \pi
ot\models\varphi , and does that action restore task-level safety? Each sub-problem is independently difficult, and their composition introduces additional challenges that no single sub-problem can resolve. Figure 1: The specification-verification-enforcement pipeline for LLM agent plans. Given a task description t t , an agent 𝒜 \mathcal{A} generates a plan π \pi . The specification stage acquires a formal safety property φ \varphi from human requirements. The verification stage checks whether π ⊧ φ \pi\models\varphi . The enforcement stage intervenes when π ⊧̸ φ \pi
ot\models\varphi . Each stage introduces independent sources of error; their composition is the central problem surveyed here. 1.2 Scope and Inclusion Criteria This survey covers: 1. LLM -based agents (single or multi-agent) that produce multi-step plans, action sequences, or tool-call chains. 2. Studies that address at least one of: plan specification, plan verification, plan enforcement, or safety monitoring. 3. Publications from 2022 to 2026, in English, across empirical, tool, survey, and position paper categories. We exclude pure chatbot safety (without a planning component), neural network verification applied to non-agent settings, and works where the LLM is an incidental Natural Language Processing (NLP) component in an otherwise classical system. 1.3 Contributions This survey makes the following contributions: 1. Systematic coverage . To the best of our knowledge, we provide the first PRISMA 2020 systematic review of the specification-verification-enforcement pipeline for LLM agent plans, identifying and synthesizing 38 studies across six databases (arXiv, ACM DL, IEEE Xplore, Semantic Scholar, Google Scholar, Preprints.org). 2. Unified taxonomy . We introduce a three-level taxonomy – paradigm, technique, system – that organizes all included works and enables direct comparison across approaches previously described in isolation (Section 4 ). 3. Comparative study . We provide a multidimensional comparison table that maps all 38 papers to formal notation, verification moment (pre-execution, runtime, post-hoc), enforcement type, task domain, tool availability, and evidence quality [ 10 ] . 4. Empirical synthesis of the verifier tax . We characterize agents along three dimensions relevant to verification. The first dimension concerns how the agent represents its plans internally and externally, as this determines which verification methods apply. Plan representation takes three forms: trace-based (interleaved thought–action–observation sequences [ 30 ] , the most common and directly amenable to LTL evaluation), graph-based (predefined or dynamic control-flow graphs suited to static analysis and DFA product construction [ 23 ] ), and code-based (executable plans verifiable via program analysis or formal contracts [ 31 , 2 ] ). A second, independent dimension is the length of plans the agent must handle, as this directly affects verification tractability. Execution horizon distinguishes short-horizon plans ( 5 to 30 5	ext{\,}30	ext{\,} actions in bounded environments such as household robotics or customer service, tractable for current verifiers) from long-horizon plans ( 50 to 500 50	ext{\,}500	ext{\,} + actions in open-ended settings such as software engineering or autonomous web navigation, beyond the reach of existing approaches). The third dimension captures whether a single agent acts in isolation or multiple agents interact, since verification complexity grows substantially with the number of agents. Agency mode ranges from single-agent systems, which produce one action sequence, to multi-agent systems, where inter-agent communication, trust delegation, and emergent interactions render per-agent verification insufficient [ 29 ] . 2.5 Foundational Definitions With the three characterization dimensions established, we now formally define the core concepts that the verification pipeline operates on. We conducted the review as an independent, rapid, systematic review from 20 to 29 May 2026; we did not pre-register it, as we note in Section 9.4 . We fixed the protocol (eligibility criteria, search strings, and synthesis approach) before beginning database searching. Eligibility criteria included publication years from 2022 to 2026 (excluding the pre- LLM -agent era before 2022), LLM -based agents producing multi-step plans, action sequences, or tool-call chains (excluding pure chatbot or dialogue safety absent planning), studies addressing plan specification, verification, enforcement, or safety monitoring (excluding neural network verification unless applied to agent plans), any study type (empirical, system/tool, survey, or position), and English-language full-text accessible papers (excluding conference abstracts without available content). We searched six databases (arXiv, ACM DL, IEEE Xplore, Semantic Scholar, Google Scholar, Preprints.org) using eight primary search strings targeting formal verification, runtime verification, temporal logic specifications, survey papers, model checking with PDDL , NL -to-formal translation, specific enforcement systems (AgentSpec, AgentGuard, VeriGuard), and roadmaps. Supplementary searches covered 22 named systems (e.g., VerifyLLM, AgentVerify, ProbGuard, LogicGuard, AgentProof, NL2LTL, LlamaFirewall) to ensure that we included systems identified during primary searching. The 38 included studies constitute the formal PRISMA corpus and form the basis for all quantitative claims, the taxonomy in Section 4 , and the GRADE assessments, while the larger reference list (64 entries) additionally includes 11 foundational references, 3 methodological references, 10 research agenda references, and 2 contextual comparison works that fall outside the PRISMA inclusion criteria; readers should therefore interpret all quantitative observations in this survey as about the 38 included studies only. 4 Taxonomy and Classification System We introduce a three-level taxonomy (Sections 4.1 to 4.3 ) classifying all 38 included studies along three orthogonal questions: when verification occurs (Level 1 – pipeline stage), what formal representation is used (Level 2 – verification moment), and how verification is performed (Level 3 – formal grounding). The three dimensions are largely independent: a runtime monitor can use temporal logic or probabilistic bounds, while a pre-execution verifier can use theorem proving or graph-automata methods. The only structural correlation is that pre-execution checking serves SPEC and VERIF, whereas ENF operates at runtime, as detailed in Table 1 . 4.1 Level 1 – Pipeline Stage 4.1.1 Specification (SPEC) Specification techniques handle how safety properties are acquired and expressed. They are the entry point of the pipeline; verification techniques consume their output. We identify three sub-categories: • SPEC- NL : NL to formal specification translation. The input is a human-expressed requirement; the output is a formula in a formal notation. Examples: NL2LTL [ 12 ] , NL2Spec [ 13 ] , NL -to- LTL / Hierarchical Semantic Decomposition (HSD) [ 33 ] , NL -to- STL [ 19 , 20 ] . • SPEC-PL : Planning language specification. The input is a task description; the output is a PDDL domain/problem or HTN description. Examples: LLMs as Planning Formalizers [ 7 ] , SayCan [ 34 ] . • SPEC-AL : Alignment-based specification. This approach encodes safety requirements as soft constraints, using training objectives or constitutions rather than formal formulas. Examples: Constitutional AI [ 35 ] , Agent Safety Alignment via Reinforcement Learning (RL) [ 36 ] . 4.1.2 Verification (VERIF) Verification techniques determine whether a plan or plan fragment satisfies a specification. We identify four sub-categories: • VERIF-MC : Model checking. The approach translates plans or plan representations to Kripke structures or FSMs; Algorithms check LTL / CTL properties. Examples: Ramani et al. [ 8 ] , AgentVerify [ 14 ] , VeriPlan [ 37 ] , Logic-based MAS Verification [ 29 ] . • VERIF-SA : Static analysis. Pre-execution structural checks on agent workflow graphs or code. Examples: AgentProof [ 23 ] , Dafny-as-IL [ 31 ] , DafnyPro [ 38 ] . • VERIF-TP : Theorem proving. Deductive verification against formal contracts. Examples: AutoRocq [ 39 ] , VeriGuard [ 2 ] . • VERIF- LLM : LLM -assisted verification. An LLM serves as a critic or judge, iteratively checking plan quality without a formal prover. Examples: Self-Refine [ 40 ] , Plan Verification via LLM -as-Judge [ 41 ] . 4.1.3 Enforcement (ENF) Enforcement techniques define what happens when verification finds a violation or anticipates one. We identify four sub-categories: • ENF-RT : Runtime monitoring and blocking: online monitors intercept unsafe actions before execution. Examples: AgentSpec [ 42 ] , Agent-C [ 3 ] , VerifyLLM [ 16 ] , LogicGuard [ 15 ] . • ENF-PROB : Probabilistic monitoring. Stochastic models forecast subsequent violations and trigger early warnings. Examples: ProbGuard [ 4 ] . • ENF-SYS : System-level guardrails. Multi-layer security infrastructure operating on prompts, reasoning traces, and generated code. Examples: LlamaFirewall [ 43 ] , Full Stack Safety [ 44 ] . • ENF-ALIGN : Alignment-based enforcement. Model training enforces safety rather than runtime checks. Examples: Constitutional AI [ 35 ] , Agent Safety Alignment via RL [ 36 ] . 4.2 Level 2 – Verification Moment The literature distinguishes three verification moments, each reflecting a different trade-off between the strength of the safety guarantee and the practical constraints of plan availability and executability. • Pre-execution verification : Means the system checks the plan in full before executing any action. This strategy permits rejection or revision before irreversible effects occur, but requires that the complete plan be available. Pre-execution verification appears in AgentProof [ 23 ] , the offline phase of VeriGuard [ 2 ] , and VerifyLLM [ 16 ] . • Runtime verification : Means the system checks each action before executing it (or at most k k steps in advance). This approach handles dynamically generated plans but cannot verify future actions that the system has not yet generated. Runtime verification appears in AgentSpec [ 42 ] , Agent-C [ 3 ] , LogicGuard [ 15 ] , and ProbGuard [ 4 ] . • Post-hoc verification : Means the system analyzes the complete execution trace after the task concludes. This approach proves useful for auditing and offline learning, but cannot prevent harm during execution. Post-hoc verification appears in Self-Refine [ 40 ] (in iterative mode) and LLM -as-Judge [ 41 ] . 4.3 Level 3 – Formal Grounding The included studies rely on several systematic and heuristic backbones. Temporal Logic uses LTL , CTL , STL , or PCTL as the specification and verification language, supporting sequential, timing, and probabilistic safety properties. It appears in the majority of included runtime monitoring systems. • Classical planning (CP) : Employs PDDL or HTN as the plan representation and verification target, enabling soundness guarantees through established plan validation tools. It appears in PDDL -survey work [ 7 ] and SayCan [ 34 ] . • Theorem proving (TP) : Relies on Coq/Rocq or Dafny as the verification backend, providing complete correctness proofs for organized programs and policies. It offers the highest assurance level but remains currently limited to code-based agents, as in AutoRocq [ 39 ] , Dafny-as-IL [ 31 ] , DafnyPro [ 38 ] , and VeriGuard [ 2 ] . • Graph and automata methods (GA) : Use DFA , FSM , or directed graph product constructions for efficient workflow-level static verification. They appear in AgentProof [ 23 ] and AgentVerify [ 14 ] . • Probabilistic methods (PR) : Draw on DTMC , MDP , or PAC -learning bounds, suiting stochastic agents where deterministic assurances remain unavailable. ProbGuard [ 4 ] illustrates this approach. • Heuristic and mixed approaches (HH) : Encompass methods without a single formal mathematical backing, including: (i) LLM -as-judge criticism (Self-Refine [ 40 ] , Plan Verification via LLM [ 41 ] ); (ii) RL reward shaping and Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback (RLAIF) / Supervised Learning from AI Feedback (SLAIF) training (Constitutional AI [ 35 ] , Agent Safety Alignment via RL [ 36 ] ); and (iii) multi-heuristic system pipelines (Full Stack Safety [ 44 ] ). Analysis of the 38 included studies reveals three representation paradigms that have emerged from the LLM -agent literature, each with distinct properties from a verification standpoint. First, trace-based representations (ReAct, Chain-of-Thought (CoT) ) use an LLM to alternate between NL “thought” steps and external “action” calls, resulting in a sequence of (thought, action, observation) triples [ 30 ] . This approach makes reasoning explicit and each plan step easy to follow, producing an execution trace suitable for LTL model checking [ 8 , 16 ] . In larger LLMs , CoT prompting [ 46 ] generates multi-step reasoning traces whose precondition–action–effect structure resembles STRIPS operator schemas [ 7 ] , allowing partial translation to classical planning formats. However, both models share a major limitation: plan correctness is only checked after the model has generated the full thought-action trace. Second, tool-augmented representations (Toolformer, SayCan) train LLMs to self-annotate Application Programming Interface (API) calls inline with NL text [ 45 ] . The resulting hybrid representation – NL interleaved with embedded API call slots – poses significant challenges for formal extraction because the boundary between specification and execution is implicit. LLM planning has been grounded in robotic affordance functions, scoring candidate actions using both language model probabilities and a skill-value function [ 34 ] . SayCan provides an implicit safety filter (the system suppresses low-affordance actions) but lacks formal guarantees; we best understand it as a learned precursor to explicit enforcement. Third, graph-based representations (LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen) represent plans as directed state graphs with typed nodes (agents, tools, and control structures) and typed edges (data movement and control flow). This representation is directly amenable to static graph analysis and product-automaton model checking [ 23 ] . A prior taxonomy classifies LLM planning into task decomposition, plan selection, external module use, and reflection/memory – each corresponding to different verification entry points [ 47 ] . Trace-based representations are the most widely studied for runtime verification, whereas graph-based representations are the most amenable to pre-deployment static analysis. Neither paradigm simultaneously supports complete pre-execution verification and arbitrary open-ended planning. The core representational gap is the absence of a canonical intermediate representation that faithfully retains both the semantic content of an LLM -generated plan and the architectural properties required for formal analysis. 5.3 Specification Techniques Formal verification requires expressing properties in a rigorous language.
